C00-1.text: How can you take the whole from the whole and still have the whole?

C00-2.text: Why does Arjuna have so many names? कौन्तेय (*Kaunteya*) and सव्यसाचिन् (*Savyasācin*) tell us different things about the same person.

C00-3.text: If वेदान्त (*Vedānta*) comes at the end, does that mean it was composed later?

C00-4.text: Ten digits can express numbers without a fixed limit. Can a small set of Sanskrit building blocks do something similar with words?

C01-1.text: Svarbhānu hides the Sun without destroying it. How does the book apply that story to Sanskrit?

C01-2.text: Sanskrit had the short word संयान (*saṃyāna*) for a train. Why were children taught a much longer word as a joke?

C01-3.text: Why was an Oxford chair of Sanskrit endowed to help convert Indians to Christianity?

C01-4.text: Vṛtra blocks the waters; Svarbhānu blocks the light. What do their actions have in common?

C02-1.text: Tamil had a detailed grammar in the *Tolkāppiyam*. Why did the language continue to change?

C02-2.text: Who kept formal Arabic stable, and what power did those institutions hold?

C02-3.text: Bṛhaspati taught Indra words for a thousand divine years and still did not finish. What was wrong with the method?

C02-4.text: Can a language keep its rules unchanged while people continue to create new words?

C03-1.text: Indra and his opponent both use माया (*māyā*). How does the listener decide which action to support?

C03-2.text: One study reviewed the arguments of thirty-five scholars about असुर (*asura*). What does the book say this debate draws attention away from?

C03-3.text: Why does the book place the swastika opposite the pyramid?

C03-4.text: What happens when आर्य (*ārya*) becomes a racial label instead of a description of conduct?

C04-1.text: Can an institution remove religious language while keeping the same arrangement of authority?

C04-2.text: A library needs copyists, buildings, and patrons. Who decides which knowledge gets copied?

C04-3.text: Why was young अष्टावक्र (*Aṣṭāvakra*) stopped at the door before he could enter the debate?

C04-4.text: Does an outsider need permission to demonstrate an error? Compare public debate with a closed review committee.

C05-1.text: Whom did Pāṇini cite when he discussed Sanskrit?

C05-2.text: Patañjali lists five reasons to study grammar. Why does protecting the Vedas come first?

C05-3.text: Does a speaker create the relationship between a word and its meaning, or use a relationship that is already established?

C05-4.text: How can a word have several meanings without its meaning simply drifting?

C06-1.text: Patañjali compares गौः (*gauḥ*) with four altered forms. How does he distinguish the established word from those forms?

C06-2.text: An accidental sound change and a deliberate attempt to erase knowledge are different threats. How can one system resist both?

C06-3.text: If two Vedic lineages recite differently, must one represent a later stage of the language?

C06-4.text: Marathi जाड (*jāḍ*) means thick or fat. How does the book connect it with Sanskrit जड (*jaḍa*)?

C07-1.text: What changes inside your mouth as you sound ॐ (*Oṃ*)?

C07-2.text: You can hold अ (*a*). What happens when you try to hold क् (*k*) in the same way?

C07-3.text: What do the tabla, bansuri, and sitar help us hear about consonants and vowels?

C07-4.text: Human beings have the same speaking organs. Why do different languages use different sets of sounds?

C08-1.text: How much of Sanskrit's basic consonant grid can Tamil, Toda, and Kurukh cover together?

C08-2.text: What do Korku, Mundari, and Ho contribute to the same comparison?

C08-3.text: Which sounds familiar in Indian speech are missing from the Central Asian languages in the comparison?

C08-4.text: Keep the mouth-place and increase the breath: क (*ka*) becomes ख (*kha*). How far does Sanskrit repeat that distinction?

C09-1.text: Why does the complete consonant grid contain two empty positions?

C09-2.text: Why does Sanskrit have no short ए (*e*) or ओ (*o*)?

C09-3.text: The Ṛgveda opens with ळ (*ḷ*) in ईळे (*īḷe*). Why is that sound outside Sanskrit's ordinary grid?

C09-4.text: Why does the sound sequence associated with Śiva's drum differ from the familiar वर्णमाला (*varṇamālā*)?

C10-1.text: गम् (*gam*), नम् (*nam*), पच् (*pac*), and वद् (*vad*) mean different things. What common shape do they share?

C10-2.text: How many recurring shapes does Sanskrit use to build its 2,168 listed धातवः (*dhātavaḥ*)?

C10-3.text: Can the individual sounds inside a धातुः (*dhātuḥ*) contribute to its meaning? Sanskrit analysts debated this.

C10-4.text: ॐ (*Oṃ*) has three sounded parts. Why do the Upaniṣads also speak of a fourth?

C10-5.text: Can the same six design tests apply to a सूत्र (*sūtra*) and to a much smaller धातुः (*dhātuḥ*)?

C11-1.text: How does भू (*bhū*), to be or become, produce भवति (*bhavati*)?

C11-2.text: Why does दा (*dā*), to give, repeat part of itself in ददाति (*dadāti*)?

C11-3.text: Where does the न् (*n*) inside रुणद्धि (*ruṇaddhi*) come from?

C11-4.text: How can a verb tell you whether someone acts, should act, or is being asked to act?

C12-1.text: What connects कर्म (*karma*), कर्तृ (*kartṛ*), and कार्य (*kārya*)?

C12-2.text: How can Sanskrit change the order of words while keeping clear who did what to whom?

C12-3.text: When a word changes its ending to indicate one, two, or many, should each form count as a new word-meaning?

C12-4.text: चन्द्रयान (*Candrayāna*) names a modern Moon mission. How can older word-building rules express something new?

C13-1.text: Can a verse carry the number 142857143 without writing a single numeral?

C13-2.text: Do you pronounce the t in “often”? Writing helped bring that sound back into speech.

C13-3.text: A page can record a sound. Can it hear whether you have pronounced that sound correctly?

C13-4.text: A stone inscription has a date. Does the knowledge written on it begin on that date?

C14-1.text: How short a break in sound can the human ear detect?

C14-2.text: Can you hear a mistake in a familiar recitation even if you cannot recite it perfectly yourself?

C14-3.text: Counting short and long syllables produces 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13. How does poetry lead to that sequence?

C14-4.text: How does the Ṛgveda describe meter, syllable, chant, and voice measuring one another?

C15-1.text: Why recite the same words forward, backward, and forward again?

C15-2.text: What mistakes can reciting words in overlapping pairs, 1–2, 2–3, 3–4, reveal that ordinary repetition might miss?

C15-3.text: Why keep both a connected recitation and a recitation that separates the words?

C15-4.text: How can teachers in distant recitation lineages check that they are passing on the same passage correctly, without one central office?

C16-1.text: रुद्रैः (*rudraiḥ*) has two syllables; रुद्रेभिः (*rudrebhiḥ*) has three. Why does the Veda need both?

C16-2.text: What breaks when the shorter ending replaces रुद्रेभिः (*rudrebhiḥ*) in its Vedic line?

C16-3.text: Can a prefix stand several words away from the verb it belongs to?

C16-4.text: Can one part of a language remain fixed while another stays open to new poetry, science, and conversation?

C17-1.text: What does repeating a word add? Try गृहे-गृहे (*gṛhe-gṛhe*), “in every house.”

C17-2.text: A sentence can put the doer at its center. Can it put the action itself there instead?

C17-3.text: “Having eaten, he came.” How does Sanskrit use one small word to show that the eating happened first?

C17-4.text: Beyond shared sounds, what do Sanskrit and Tamil show about who keeps knowledge alive?

C18-1.text: If an account explains where people traveled, has it also explained how Sanskrit was built and maintained?

C18-2.text: Creating a language is one task. What would it take to keep that language usable for thousands of years?

C18-3.text: Why does सत् (*sat*) need a long memory?

C18-4.text: Can praising Pāṇini hide the achievement of the people before him?

C19-1.text: How do you write a fable in a reconstructed language with no recorded speakers?

C19-2.text: When a dictionary says “from PIE” and places an asterisk before the reconstructed word, what do the word “from” and the star each tell the reader?

C19-3.text: Look up “king” in dictionaries from different generations. What happened to जनक (*janaka*) in the explanation?

C19-4.text: Can a word pass into another language without the speakers of the source language moving there?

C20-1.text: What are names associated with Mitra and Varuṇa doing in a treaty from West Asia?

C20-2.text: Say ध्यान (*dhyāna*), Chan, and Zen. What changed as the word traveled?

C20-3.text: Why is the Japanese “fifty sounds” table a grid?

C20-4.text: A language can borrow a way of studying sounds, not just a list of words. What did Chinese scholars build from that encounter?

F-1.text: How did a mother's correction of one sound become the beginning of this book?

F-2.text: The मूर्ति (*mūrti*) does not tell the seeker what to do. How can it still guide conduct?

F-3.text: What do the eleven blocks hiding the Sun represent?

E-1.text: Why can the person who receives भिक्षा (*bhikṣā*) not demand it?

E-2.text: Does keeping Sanskrit stable require freezing Marathi, Tamil, or other living languages?

E-3.text: Can anyone become आर्य (*ārya*)? What would that require them to do?

A01-1.text: Can you follow the change in a dictionary explanation entry by entry, instead of accepting a general claim about it?

A02-1.text: In 1948, an Indian Sanskrit dictionary project adopted the historical method of an English dictionary. What did that choice assume?

A03-1.text: If two scripts have similar-looking signs, does that explain how they represent sounds?

A04-1.text: Does the sound comparison change when different Indian and external language groups are tested?

A05-1.text: What happens if you put Japanese sounds through Sanskrit's word-building rules?

A06-1.text: Which sounds appear most often at the beginning of a Sanskrit atom, and which occur most often at its end?

A07-1.text: You may know the गायत्री (*Gāyatrī*) mantra by heart. How are its words built and joined?

A08-1.text: A Vedic prefix can stand apart from its verb even in prose. What keeps the connection clear when meter is not involved?

A09-1.text: What evidence would distinguish a permitted alternative from a form that changed over time?

A10-1.text: Why does this book introduce words such as “sonomer” and “auditure”?
A10-1.reference: Appendix Part 10, “Why This Book Coins Terms”
